name: Ring-necked Snake
habitat: Moist woodland, rocky hillsides, gardens and grassland, under logs, bark and stones
range: Most of the USA and south-eastern Canada, from Nova Scotia to Florida and west to the Pacific coast; into Mexico
diet: Salamanders, earthworms, slugs and small snakes
active: Mostly at night; under cover by day
ids: A small, slim snake, grey, black or olive above, with a bright yellow or orange ring around the neck.
The belly is bright yellow, orange or red, often with small black dots.
When disturbed it coils its tail into a corkscrew to flash the red underside.
Smooth scales and a small, flat head.

look.colour: Grey, black or olive; neck ring and belly yellow, orange or red
look.pattern: Plain, with a bright neck ring
look.head: Small and flat, with a bright collar behind it

fact: Its saliva subdues salamanders, but it is far too small and gentle to harm people.

name: Eastern Wormsnake
habitat: Damp woodland and forest edges, under logs, stones and leaf litter
range: The eastern USA from Massachusetts to Georgia, west to Illinois and Alabama
ids: A tiny, plain brown snake that looks like an earthworm.
A pink belly, the pink reaching only the lowest row of side scales.
Smooth, shiny scales, a pointed head and a tail tipped with a small spine.
fact: It presses the spine on its tail tip into your hand when picked up; it cannot sting.

name: Western Wormsnake
habitat: Damp woodland, rocky hillsides and forest edges
range: The central USA: Missouri, Arkansas, Kansas, Oklahoma, Iowa, Illinois and Louisiana
ids: A tiny, worm-like snake: dark purplish-black above and pink below.
The pink reaches up onto the lower sides.
Smooth, shiny scales and a spine on the tail tip.
fact: It is a western twin of the Eastern Wormsnake, darker on the back.

name: Red-bellied Mudsnake
habitat: Swamps, marshes, slow streams and cypress ponds
range: The south-east and Mississippi valley: Virginia to Florida, west to Texas and north to southern Illinois
ids: Large and glossy black above, with red or pink bars rising onto the sides from the belly.
A red-and-black checkered belly.
A short tail ending in a sharp spine.

look.colour: Glossy black with red or pink
look.pattern: Red bars on the sides; checkered belly
look.head: Small and rounded

fact: The legend of the "hoop snake" that rolls with its tail in its mouth comes from this harmless snake.

name: Rainbow Snake
habitat: Blackwater rivers, swamps and coastal marshes
range: The south-eastern coastal plain from Virginia to Florida and Louisiana
ids: Glossy blue-black with three red stripes along the back.
Yellow and red on the sides and belly, with rows of black spots.
A pointed tail spine.
fact: It eats almost nothing but eels and is rarely seen out of the water.

name: Common Sharp-tailed Snake
habitat: Moist woodland, grassland edges and rocky hillsides, under logs and stones
range: The Pacific coast: California, Oregon, Washington and southern British Columbia
active: Active in cool, wet weather; hidden in summer
ids: A small reddish-brown or grey snake with a sharp spine at the tip of its tail.
A belly with bold black and white crossbars.
Smooth scales and a small head.
fact: Its long teeth are made for gripping slippery slugs.

name: Forest Sharp-tailed Snake
habitat: Moist coastal forests
range: Northern California and south-western Oregon
ids: Like the Common Sharp-tailed Snake but with a longer tail.
Reddish-brown with a spine on the tail tip and a barred belly.

look.head: Small
look.body: Small and slim, with a long tail

fact: It was described as a separate species only in 2010.

name: Desert Nightsnake
habitat: Deserts, sagebrush, rocky hillsides and grassland
range: The Great Basin and desert south-west: Washington and Idaho to Nevada, Utah, Arizona and California; into Mexico
diet: Lizards, their eggs and small frogs
ids: A small, pale grey or tan snake with rows of dark brown blotches.
Large dark patches on the neck, and a dark stripe behind each eye.
Vertical (cat-like) pupils and a flat head.

look.colour: Pale grey, tan or cream with brown blotches
look.head: Flat, with vertical pupils

fact: Its vertical pupils make it look like a tiny viper, but it is harmless to people.

name: Chihuahuan Nightsnake
habitat: Desert, grassland, rocky hillsides and canyons
range: The southern plains and Chihuahuan Desert: Kansas, Colorado, Oklahoma, New Mexico, Texas and Arizona; into Mexico
diet: Lizards, their eggs, frogs and small snakes
ids: A small, light grey or tan snake with dark brown blotches.
Dark neck patches and a dark stripe behind the eye.
Vertical pupils.

look.colour: Light grey or tan with brown blotches
look.head: Flat, with vertical pupils

fact: It is the eastern member of the nightsnake group, reaching the Kansas prairies.

name: Coast Nightsnake
habitat: Coastal scrub, chaparral, rocky hillsides and grassland
range: Coastal and southern California; into Baja California
diet: Lizards and their eggs, and frogs
ids: A small, light grey or beige snake with dark brown blotches.
Dark neck patches and a dark stripe through the eye.
Vertical pupils.
fact: Like all nightsnakes, it hides under rocks by day and is often found on roads at night.

name: Sonoran Lyresnake
habitat: Rocky desert hillsides, canyons and cliffs
range: Arizona, south-eastern California, Nevada, south-western Utah and New Mexico; into Mexico
ids: Light brown or grey with dark brown saddles that have pale centres.
A lyre- or V-shaped dark mark on top of the head.
Vertical pupils and a broad head on a thin neck.

look.head: Broad, with a V-shaped mark and vertical pupils

fact: It climbs rock crevices to catch roosting bats.

name: California Lyresnake
habitat: Rocky hillsides, canyons and chaparral
range: Southern California; into Baja California
ids: Pale grey-brown with dark brown, pale-centred blotches.
A dark lyre-shaped mark on the head.
Vertical pupils.

look.head: Broad, with a lyre mark and vertical pupils

fact: It was split from the Sonoran Lyresnake on the basis of its DNA.

name: Texas Lyresnake
habitat: Rocky desert mountains and canyons
range: West Texas and southern New Mexico; into Mexico
ids: Grey with widely spaced dark brown crossbands.
A faint lyre mark on the head and vertical pupils.
fact: It is one of the least-seen snakes of the Big Bend region.

name: Flat-headed Snake
habitat: Rocky hillsides, woodland and grassland, under stones and logs
range: The south-central USA: Missouri, Arkansas, Kansas, Oklahoma, Louisiana and Texas
ids: A tiny, plain tan or grey-brown snake with a slightly darker, flattened head.
No sharp black cap, unlike the black-headed snakes.
A pink or salmon belly.
fact: It hunts centipedes under rocks, subduing them with a very mild venom.

name: Plains Black-headed Snake
habitat: Prairie, desert grassland and rocky hillsides
range: The southern plains: Kansas, Colorado, Oklahoma, Texas, New Mexico and Arizona; into Mexico
ids: A tiny tan snake with a black cap on the head that ends in a point on the neck.
No pale collar behind the cap.
A pink belly.
fact: It is the black-headed snake of the Great Plains.

name: Southeastern Crowned Snake
habitat: Dry woodland, pine forest and sandy hillsides
range: The south-east: Virginia to north Florida, west to Mississippi and Kentucky
ids: A tiny tan or reddish-brown snake with a black head.
A pale band across the back of the head, then a black collar.
Smooth scales and a white belly.

look.pattern: Plain, with a black head and collar
look.head: Black, with a pale band behind it

fact: The pale band between the black cap and the black collar is its "crown".

name: Southwestern Black-headed Snake
habitat: Desert, grassland and rocky canyons
range: The south-west: Arizona, Utah, Nevada, California, New Mexico and west Texas; into Mexico
ids: A tiny light brown or beige snake with a black cap.
Often a faint pale collar behind the cap.
A pink or orange stripe along the belly.
fact: It is named after the American herpetologist Hobart M. Smith.

name: Western Black-headed Snake
habitat: Grassland, chaparral, woodland and rocky hillsides
range: Coastal and southern California; into Baja California
ids: A tiny olive-brown snake with a black cap that ends in a straight edge or points a little down the neck.
Often a thin pale collar behind the cap.
A pink or orange belly.
fact: It is California's commonest black-headed snake, but few people ever see one.

name: Florida Crowned Snake
habitat: Sand pine scrub, sandhills and coastal dunes
range: Florida and southern Georgia
ids: A tiny tan snake with a black head; in some forms a pale band crosses the head.
A white belly.
Burrows in loose sand.
fact: It "swims" through loose sand in the Florida scrub.

name: Trans-Pecos Black-headed Snake
habitat: Rocky desert mountains and grassland
range: West Texas; into Mexico
active: Hidden under cover; out after rain
ids: A small tan snake with a large black hood covering the head and neck.
The hood may have a pale collar across it.
fact: The largest black-headed snake in the USA, found only in the Big Bend region.

name: Yaqui Black-headed Snake
habitat: Rocky canyons and oak woodland
range: South-eastern Arizona and south-western New Mexico; into Mexico
ids: A tiny brown snake with a black cap, a white collar and a black band behind it.
White patches on the cheeks.

look.pattern: Plain, with a black cap and white collar
look.head: Black, with white cheeks

fact: In the USA it lives only in a few canyons near the border.

name: Great Plains Groundsnake
habitat: Prairie, rocky hillsides and desert grassland, under rocks
range: The southern plains: Kansas, Colorado, Oklahoma, Texas and New Mexico
ids: A small, very variable snake: plain brown, orange or grey, striped, or banded with black.
Often a dark spot at the front edge of each scale.
Smooth, glossy scales and a small head.
fact: Snakes from the same rock can look completely different: one plain, one striped, one banded.

name: Western Groundsnake
habitat: Desert, rocky hillsides and grassland
range: The Great Basin and south-west: Oregon, Idaho, Nevada, Utah, California and Arizona; into Mexico
ids: Very variable: plain orange, grey or brown, striped, or banded with black and orange.
Smooth, glossy scales.
Small and slim with a small head.

look.colour: Orange, grey, brown, or banded black and orange
look.head: Small

fact: Its banded form is a coral-snake look-alike, but most have no bands at all.

name: Western Shovel-nosed Snake
habitat: Sandy desert, dunes and washes
range: The Mojave and Sonoran Deserts of California, Nevada and Arizona; into Mexico
ids: Cream or yellow with black bands (and sometimes red patches between them).
A flat, shovel-shaped snout for swimming through sand.
Smooth, glossy scales.

look.colour: Cream or yellow with black bands, sometimes red
look.head: Flat and shovel-shaped

fact: It "swims" through loose sand, with its jaw countersunk below its snout to keep the sand out.

name: Colorado Desert Shovel-nosed Snake
habitat: Sandy desert and dunes
range: South-eastern California and western Arizona; into Mexico
ids: Cream or yellowish with black rings and red patches between them.
A flat, shovel-shaped snout.
Smooth, glossy scales.
fact: Its bright bands look like a coral snake's, though it is harmless.

name: Variable Sandsnake
habitat: Sandy desert flats and washes
range: Southern Arizona; into Mexico
ids: Tiny, cream or orange with black crossbands (some have none).
A flattened, shovel-like snout and a deeply sunk lower jaw.
Smooth, glossy scales.
fact: It moves through sand so smoothly that it barely leaves a trace on the surface.

name: South Texas Groundsnake
habitat: Thornscrub and sandy brushland
range: South Texas; into north-eastern Mexico
ids: A tiny brown or tan snake, sometimes with a faint pale stripe.
Smooth, glossy scales and a small head.
fact: It was long treated as part of the Western Groundsnake.

name: Spotted Leaf-nosed Snake
habitat: Sandy and gravelly desert flats
range: The Mojave and Sonoran Deserts of California, Nevada and Arizona; into Mexico
ids: Pale pinkish or tan with many dark brown blotches.
A large, leaf-shaped scale on the tip of the snout.
Vertical pupils and a blunt head.

look.head: Blunt, with a leaf-like snout scale

fact: It uses its enlarged snout scale to dig up buried lizard eggs.

name: Saddled Leaf-nosed Snake
habitat: Sonoran Desert flats and foothills
range: South-central Arizona; into Mexico
ids: Pinkish or cream with large, dark brown saddles.
A leaf-shaped scale on the snout.
Vertical pupils.

look.colour: Pink or cream with brown saddles
look.head: Blunt, with a leaf-like snout scale

fact: Its fewer, larger saddles tell it apart from the Spotted Leaf-nosed Snake.

name: Chihuahuan Hook-nosed Snake
habitat: Desert grassland and rocky hillsides
range: West Texas, southern New Mexico and south-eastern Arizona; into Mexico
ids: A small, stout snake with an upturned, hooked snout.
Grey or tan with brown crossbands.
Makes popping sounds from its vent when alarmed.

look.colour: Grey or tan with brown bands
look.head: With an upturned hook on the snout

fact: Its alarm "pop" is made by pushing air out of its vent.

name: Tamaulipan Hook-nosed Snake
habitat: Thornscrub and brushland
range: The lower Rio Grande valley of Texas; into Mexico
ids: A small grey snake with faint dark crossbars.
A sharply upturned, pointed snout.
fact: It is mostly seen on roads after heavy rain in south Texas.

name: Pine Woods Littersnake
habitat: Pine flatwoods and hammocks, under bark and in leaf litter
range: The south-eastern coastal plain from North Carolina to Florida and Louisiana
ids: A small, glossy golden-brown or reddish snake.
A dark stripe through the eye and pale lips.
A plain yellowish belly.

look.head: Small, with a dark eye stripe

fact: Its mild venom helps it overpower small frogs; it is harmless to people.

name: Northern Cat-eyed Snake
habitat: Thornscrub, woodland and stream edges
range: The lower Rio Grande valley of Texas; through Mexico to Central America
ids: Tan or yellowish with large dark brown saddles.
Large eyes with vertical pupils.
A broad head on a slim neck.

look.colour: Tan or yellow with dark saddles
look.head: Broad, with big cat-like eyes

fact: It climbs into trees over ponds to eat frog eggs laid on leaves.

name: Black-striped Snake
habitat: Thornscrub, woodland and gardens
range: The lower Rio Grande valley of Texas; through Mexico to Central America
ids: Brown with three dark stripes along the back.
A pale stripe from the snout over the eye.
A red or orange belly.

look.colour: Brown with dark stripes; red belly
look.head: With a pale stripe over the eye

fact: Its bite can cause pain and swelling, so it is best left alone.

name: Thornscrub Vinesnake
habitat: Oak woodland, thornscrub and canyons
range: South-central Arizona; into Mexico
active: By day, in bushes and trees
ids: Extremely thin, grey or brown, like a twig or vine.
A long, pointed head.
A dark stripe through the eye.
fact: It holds perfectly still among branches, looking just like a dead twig.

name: Northern Rubber Boa
habitat: Moist forests, woodland, meadows and rocky hillsides
range: The west: British Columbia, Washington, Oregon, Idaho, Montana, Wyoming, Utah, Nevada and California
diet: Baby mice and shrews, and lizards
ids: A short, thick snake with smooth, rubbery-looking skin: plain olive, brown or tan above, yellow below.
A blunt tail shaped like its head.
When threatened it hides its head in its coils and waves its tail like a fake head.

look.colour: Plain olive, brown or tan; yellow below
look.head: Small and blunt, like the tail

fact: Many rubber boas have scarred tails from mother mice biting the decoy "head" while the boa eats their young.

name: Southern Rubber Boa
habitat: Mountain forests
range: The San Bernardino and San Jacinto Mountains of southern California
ids: A short, rubbery-looking boa, plain brown to pinkish-tan.
A blunt tail like the head.
fact: It is a threatened species known from just two mountain ranges.

name: Rosy Boa
habitat: Rocky desert hillsides, canyons and coastal sage scrub
range: Southern California, Arizona and southern Nevada; into Mexico
ids: A heavy, slow boa with three broad stripes along the body: rosy, orange, reddish-brown or grey on a cream, grey or bluish background.
Small, smooth scales and tiny eyes.
A blunt head barely wider than the neck.

look.colour: Grey, cream or bluish with rosy, orange or brown stripes
look.head: Blunt, with small eyes

fact: One of only two boa species native to the USA, along with the rubber boas.

name: Three-lined Boa
habitat: Rocky desert and thornscrub
range: South-western Arizona; into Sonora and Baja California
ids: Three bold dark brown or black stripes on a cream or pale grey body.
Smooth scales, small eyes and a blunt head.

look.colour: Cream or pale grey with dark stripes
look.head: Blunt

fact: In the USA it is found only in the Organ Pipe Cactus area of Arizona.

name: Texas Threadsnake
habitat: Grassland, rocky hillsides and gardens with loose soil
range: Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, New Mexico and Arizona; into Mexico
diet: Ants and termites, their larvae and pupae
active: Underground; on the surface after rain
ids: A tiny, shiny pinkish-brown snake as thin as a strand of spaghetti, looking like an earthworm.
Its eyes are just dark spots under the head scales.
Blunt at both ends, with a tiny spine on the tail.
fact: Screech owls carry live threadsnakes to their nests, where the snakes eat the insects that would harm the chicks.

name: Western Threadsnake
habitat: Desert and scrub with loose soil, rock crevices and washes
range: The south-west: California, Nevada, Utah, Arizona, New Mexico and west Texas; into Mexico
active: Underground; on the surface on warm nights
ids: A tiny, shiny, worm-like snake, purplish-brown or pink above and paler below.
Eyes are dark spots under the scales.
Blunt head and tail.
fact: It follows the scent trails of ants to find their nests.
